chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Board, the Auditor and the Pay Packet

lessons.title: Case Study: When the Auditor Walks Out

body.text: An auditor resigning is a professional giving up fees because staying has become riskier than leaving. It is the loudest thing an auditor can say without saying it.

children.text: In Lesson 9 you learned the rules around auditor changes. This case study looks at what actually happened when large audit firms walked away from Indian listed companies, what the companies said in response, and what followed. The pattern is remarkably consistent, and once you have seen it three times you will recognise it the fourth.

For years, walking away from a large client was rare. Two changes in 2018 shifted the maths. In January 2018, SEBI barred Price Waterhouse network firms from auditing listed companies for two years over the Satyam audits, showing that signing off on bad numbers could cost a firm an entire market. Later that year, the government set up the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) as an independent regulator for auditors of listed and large companies. Suddenly, the risk of staying with a client that would not provide evidence was far higher than the loss of one audit fee. Resignations at listed companies rose sharply through 2018 and 2019.

body.text: Think about what an auditor gives up by resigning: a fee that recurs every year, a client relationship, and usually the chance to bid for work from the rest of that business group. When a large firm accepts all of that rather than sign one more report, take it seriously.

children.text: Manpasand Beverages, a Vadodara-based maker of fruit drinks best known for its Mango Sip brand, was a small cap growth favourite. It listed in 2015 and reported rapid revenue growth as it expanded distribution and capacity, attracting mutual funds and retail investors.

body.title: Manpasand Beverages: from growth story to auditor exit

events.title: IPO at ₹320 per share
events.description: The company lists on NSE and BSE and is quickly re-rated as a fast-growing consumer business.

events.title: Rapid reported growth
events.description: Revenue and profit rise quickly, and the company raises further capital from institutional investors to fund expansion.

events.title: Deloitte resigns just before annual results
events.description: Statutory auditor Deloitte Haskins & Sells resigns, saying key information it needed to complete the audit had not been provided. The stock falls sharply in the following sessions.

events.title: New auditor appointed, results declared
events.description: The company appoints a new, smaller audit firm and publishes its results. Management maintains the business is sound. Investor confidence does not return.

events.title: Promoter-MD arrested by GST authorities
events.description: GST intelligence officials arrest the managing director and others in a case of alleged fake invoicing. The stock goes on to lose most of its value.

children.text: A year separated the auditor's warning from the enforcement action. Shareholders who treated the resignation as the end of trust had that whole year to exit. Shareholders who waited for proof got the proof, at a much lower price.

Reliance Capital was the financial services flagship of the Anil Dhirubhai Ambani Group, with interests spanning lending, insurance, and asset management. This was not an obscure small cap. It was a large, well-known group company.

body.title: Reliance Capital: the auditor's concerns and what followed

events.title: PwC resigns as statutory auditor
events.description: Price Waterhouse & Co resigns as auditor of Reliance Capital and its subsidiary Reliance Home Finance, saying it had raised concerns about certain transactions with the audit committee and they had not been satisfactorily addressed.

events.title: Company publicly disputes the auditor
events.description: Reliance Capital rejects the auditor's concerns as unfounded and says it had responded to all queries.

events.title: Defaults and downgrades
events.description: Group lending entities face mounting stress, credit rating downgrades, and defaults on borrowings.

events.title: RBI supersedes the board
events.description: RBI replaces Reliance Capital's board with an administrator and moves the company into insolvency proceedings.

body.text: Notice the company's response. A listed company publicly contradicting its own departing auditor is itself a governance signal. The auditor has professional liability, regulatory oversight, and nothing to gain from inventing concerns. Management has every incentive to minimise them. When the two accounts conflict, give far more weight to the auditor's.

children.text: Vakrangee, which ran a network of rural retail and banking service outlets, had been one of the biggest stock market winners of 2017, with its market value climbing to tens of thousands of crores by early 2018. The stock was already falling amid questions about its business and trading in its shares when, in April 2018, statutory auditor Price Waterhouse resigned, saying information it had sought, including on parts of the business, had not been provided. The stock continued to fall and lost most of its value over the following months.

cells: Concerns raised with audit committee not addressed
Arrests over alleged fake invoicing a year later
Continued fall; the stock lost most of its value

body.title: What the Resignation Told You vs What Came Later

columns.label: Known on the Day of Resignation
points: A reputable firm would not sign the next report
The reason involved missing information or unresolved concerns, not a scheduled rotation
Management's explanation contradicted or minimised the auditor's

columns.label: Confirmed Months or Years Later
points: Specific transactions or balances the auditor could not verify
Regulatory findings on disclosures or trading
Most of the market value gone

children.text: The left column was enough. You did not need to know what the auditor had found. You needed to accept that the one independent party checking the numbers had refused to keep checking them.

Since SEBI's October 2019 circular, the company must disclose the auditor's detailed reasons for resigning, and the audit committee must share its views. So today you get the auditor's own words on the exchange the same day or soon after. Here is how to read them.

body.caption: Resignation reasons, from least to most serious

cells: Completion of term or mandatory rotation
Routine; confirm the dates match Section 139 limits
Group auditor alignment after an acquisition or merger
Normal when a new parent brings in its own auditor; check that the acquisition actually happened
Often vague. Check whether the company is small enough for fees to be a real issue, and read the audit committee's views
Concerns raised with management or audit committee not resolved
The auditor is on record that it raised specific issues; find out what they were
Information or evidence requested was not provided
Management chose not to show the auditor something. Assume the reported numbers are unverified
The auditor may be required to report fraud to the government under Section 143(12). Treat the accounts as unreliable

body.title: Rank the Letter
body.question: Which phrase in an auditor's resignation letter should worry a shareholder the most?
options: 'We have completed our second term as statutory auditors in accordance with Section 139.'
'Due to pre-occupation with other assignments, we are unable to continue.'
'Despite repeated requests, we have not been provided with the underlying documents supporting certain balances and transactions with related parties.'
'Following the acquisition of the Company by its new parent, we understand the Group wishes to align its auditors.'
body.explanation: Options A and D describe routine, verifiable reasons. Option B is vague and worth probing, but does not accuse anyone of anything. Option C says management refused to show the auditor evidence for related party balances and transactions, which is precisely where value leakage hides. That is the language of an auditor who cannot stand behind the numbers.

children.text: Why Waiting for Clarity Is Expensive

When a serious resignation hits a small or mid cap, the stock can be locked at its lower price band for several sessions with almost no buyers. You cannot sell at any price until the band opens. The common instinct is to wait for management to explain. By the time an explanation arrives, the price has usually already moved.

body.title: Three Lower Circuits
body.prompt: A stock with a 20% price band closes at ₹500 the day before its auditor resigns citing information not provided. It then hits its 20% lower circuit on three consecutive sessions, with each session's band applied to the previous close. What is the closing price after the third session?
body.explanation: ₹500 × 0.8 = ₹400, then ₹400 × 0.8 = ₹320, then ₹320 × 0.8 = ₹256. That is a 48.8% fall in three sessions, and on lower circuit days sell orders pile up with few buyers, so most holders cannot exit even at those prices. Deciding your response on the day of the resignation, not after the explanation, is what protects you.

body.title: Resignation Day
body.scenario: You hold a mid cap specialty chemicals company listed on NSE. It is 20 May, ten days before the deadline for annual results. At 9:05 am, the company files the resignation of its statutory auditor, a large firm in the third year of its first term. The auditor's reasons: 'We have not received satisfactory responses and supporting documents for inter-corporate deposits of ₹620 crore placed with entities we understand to be related to the promoter group, and for the business rationale of certain purchase transactions.' The company's accompanying statement says the auditor's observations are 'procedural in nature' and that it will appoint a new auditor shortly. The company's net worth is ₹2,100 crore. Last year's audit report had a Key Audit Matter on 'recoverability of inter-corporate deposits'. The stock opens at its 20% lower circuit.
body.prompt: What do you do today, and what would have to be true for you to consider holding?
body.modelAnswer: Treat this as a very high severity resignation. The auditor names a specific amount, ₹620 crore, which is about 30% of net worth, placed with entities it believes are promoter-related, and says it was not given documents. That is not procedural. Last year's Key Audit Matter on the same deposits shows the concern has been building. The company's 'procedural' framing contradicts the auditor's language, which is a second red flag. Today, place a sell order and keep it in the queue, accepting that it may not execute until the circuit opens, rather than waiting for the company's explanation. Also read the audit committee's views when filed and check the related party note and CARO clause 3(iii) from last year to identify the counterparties. You would only consider holding if the deposits were repaid in cash and verified by a new, credible auditor of similar standing, the audit committee's independent members publicly confirmed the concerns were resolved, and the next audit opinion came back unmodified. Until then, the reported net worth cannot be relied on.

body.title: When an auditor change really is harmless

children.text: Not every departure is a warning. Rotation at the end of a five or ten year tenure is required by law. After an acquisition, a new parent often brings the subsidiary onto its own global auditor. Small companies sometimes genuinely cannot afford a large firm's fees. Three checks separate these from the cases above: the reason is specific and verifiable, the audit committee's views confirm there were no unresolved concerns, and the previous audit reports were clean with no Emphasis of Matter or related party Key Audit Matters. If all three hold, note the change and move on.

body.title: Your Auditor Resignation Response Plan
steps: Set an alert for corporate announcements on BSE or NSE, or a watchlist alert on screener.in, for every stock you hold
When a resignation is filed, read the auditor's own reasons before the company's statement
Place the reason on the severity table: rotation and group alignment are low; unresolved concerns, missing information, or fraud are high to severe
Check whether the auditor's words and the company's explanation agree
Pull up the last two or three audit reports for qualifications, Emphasis of Matter, or Key Audit Matters on related parties, loans, or receivables
Note who replaces the auditor, how quickly, and whether the new firm has comparable listed clients
For high severity reasons, decide your action the same day rather than waiting for management's explanation

body.text: This case study is based on exchange filings, regulatory actions, and widely reported events. It describes allegations and outcomes as publicly reported and makes no finding of wrongdoing beyond those. It is for education only and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: SEBI's 2018 ban on Price Waterhouse network firms and the creation of NFRA raised the cost of signing doubtful accounts, triggering a wave of auditor resignations in 2018 and 2019

Manpasand Beverages, Reliance Capital, and Vakrangee followed one pattern: a large firm resigns near results, cites missing information or unresolved concerns, management minimises it, and serious trouble follows
When the auditor's reasons and management's explanation conflict, give far more weight to the auditor
Resignation reasons range from routine rotation to 'information not provided' and reported fraud; only the first few are harmless
Lower circuits can trap holders for days, so decide your response on the day of a serious resignation, not after management explains
Check prior audit reports: related party Key Audit Matters or Emphasis of Matter paragraphs usually show the concern was building before the auditor left
